passage:
Thursday
Keerthana failed the chem retest. Honestly, it was so obvious. She went to her cousin's wedding in Salem the weekend before, three days of dancing, and came back saying she'd manage. Anyone could have seen that coming. I told Divya at lunch, "I knew it the second she said wedding."
Although. Now that I write it: when she told me about the wedding two weeks ago, I said, "Go, you've studied loads, you'll be fine." I even helped her pick a dupatta. She had done every past paper. Last time she did the same and scored 78.
Still. It was kind of obvious. Wasn't it?
Rekha

qa.q: What did Rekha say when Keerthana first mentioned the wedding?
qa.a: "Go, you've studied loads, you'll be fine."

qa.q: Why does the failure feel so obvious to Rekha now?
qa.a: Knowing the result makes the wedding look like a clear mistake, so Rekha feels sure and a little superior, forgetting how relaxed the plan seemed beforehand.

qa.q: What could Rekha ask before calling it obvious?
qa.a: What Keerthana knew before the exam, like every past paper done and a 78 last time, and whether anyone, including Rekha, expected a fail.

qa.q: How might Keerthana feel if she heard her failure called obvious?
qa.a: She would likely feel hurt and judged unfairly, since the choice looked reasonable to both of them at the time.

grounding: A teenager's diary calls a friend's exam failure obvious, though the diary itself shows the outcome looked open beforehand.

passage:
Faculty adviser's note, college cultural committee review, 18 February
The committee met to review the outdoor music night that was cancelled when the rain came. Most members said the risk was obvious and that Imran, who chose the open ground, should have known. Imran said little. Tanvir, the committee secretary, asked to see the notes from the planning meeting in January. He read out what the group had known then: the forecast showed clear skies, the indoor hall was booked by the exam cell, and every member had voted yes. He asked, "Given what we had that day, what would a better choice have been?" Nobody had an answer. The review turned to planning: a rain-backup clause for future bookings. I suggested we keep dated planning notes for every event.

qa.q: What did the forecast show in January?
qa.a: Clear skies.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir ask to see the January notes?
qa.a: He seemed uneasy that Imran was being blamed with hindsight, and wanted the review to be fair to what was known when the choice was made.

qa.q: How did the review change after Tanvir's question, and why is that better?
qa.a: It moved from blaming Imran to planning a rain-backup clause, which helps future events instead of punishing a reasonable choice.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Imran before Tanvir spoke?
qa.a: Imran probably felt blamed and ashamed, staying quiet while others called the risk obvious.

grounding: A faculty adviser records a student secretary asking what was known when a failed event was planned, instead of joining the blame.

passage:
Monday night
NSS review meeting today about the blood donation camp that got only eleven donors. Within five minutes everyone was saying, "Obviously nobody comes during mid-sems, Vikas should have known." Vikas kept staring at the table.
I almost joined in. Then I remembered: when he proposed the date in August, the mid-sem schedule wasn't even out. The exam cell posted it three weeks later. And last year's camp in the same week had forty donors.
So I said that. Out loud. My voice shook a little. I asked, "What did we actually know when we picked the date?" It went quiet, then Pooja said, "Nothing about exams." We ended up making a rule to check the academic calendar before fixing dates, instead of blaming Vikas.
He messaged me later: "thanks." Just that.
Avni

qa.q: How many donors came to the camp?
qa.a: Only eleven donors.

qa.q: How did Avni feel speaking up in the meeting?
qa.a: Avni felt nervous, with a shaking voice, but also uneasy about Vikas being blamed for something no one could have known in August.

qa.q: What rule came out of the meeting, and why is it more useful than blame?
qa.a: Checking the academic calendar before fixing dates, which prevents the problem next time without punishing a choice made before the schedule was out.

qa.q: What might the one-word thanks say about how Vikas felt?
qa.a: Vikas probably felt relieved and grateful that someone stood up for him, even if he didn't have words for more.

grounding: A student in a review meeting asks what was known when a failed camp's date was chosen, instead of calling the risk obvious.

passage:
Wednesday
The school-enrolment drive in Ward 9 flopped: 14 families signed up, and we'd hoped for 60. At the review, Mr Sen started with, "Farida should have known Ward 9 was difficult."
I opened the decision log. In March we had written: "Ward 9 chosen: highest number of out-of-school kids, community leader supportive. Risk: monsoon may start early. Our guess: 50 to 70 families, 60% sure." Then the monsoon came two weeks early and the leader moved away. Farida's plan was sound; our information and luck changed.
Mr Sen read it twice and said, "Okay, so it's the backup plan we lacked, not Farida." That's the review I wanted.
Note to self: keep writing these before every decision. Today it saved a good person from blame.
Joseph

qa.q: How many families signed up in Ward 9?
qa.a: 14 families.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after the review?
qa.a: Joseph felt relieved and satisfied that the log showed the plan was sound, saving Farida from unfair blame.

qa.a: The decision log written in March recorded reasons, risks and a guess before the outcome; other teams could write one before every decision.

qa.q: What might Farida have felt when Mr Sen began the review?
qa.a: Farida may have felt anxious and blamed, since the review opened by saying Farida should have known.

grounding: A young lead's diary shows a decision log written before the outcome letting a review separate sound planning from bad luck.

passage: The farmer cooperative's office in Bankura smelled of jute sacks. This season's new paddy variety had failed on half the plots, and members were angry. "Preeti madam pushed this seed," someone shouted. "Anyone could see it was risky." Arnab, the secretary, didn't argue. He opened the red register where, every June, he wrote down each decision before sowing. He read aloud: "New variety on forty plots. Reason: resists the pest that hit us last year. Risk: needs steady rain. Rain forecast: normal. Our guess: good yield, seven chances in ten." He looked up. "The rain stopped for three weeks in August. None of us knew that in June." The room grew quieter. An old farmer nodded slowly. "Then next year, some plots old seed, some new." Preeti, at the back, finally unclenched her hands.

qa.q: What reason did the register give for choosing the new variety?
qa.a: It resists the pest that hit them last year.

qa.q: Why did Arnab open the red register instead of arguing?
qa.a: He felt calm and wanted fairness, trusting that the reasons written in June would show the choice was sensible, not careless.

qa.q: What lesson did the old farmer draw, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Planting some plots with old seed and some with new next year, which learns from the result without blaming anyone for luck.

qa.q: What might Preeti have felt as the room grew quieter?
qa.a: Preeti likely felt relieved, unclenching her hands once the register showed the blame was unfair.

grounding: A cooperative secretary reads out reasons and forecasts written before sowing, so a failed crop is reviewed without wrongly blaming the officer.

passage: Last Sunday at the fair, I bought a big cone of candy floss with my own pocket money. After four bites it was too sweet and my teeth felt funny. But it had cost thirty rupees, so I kept eating. My sister Sonali said, "Joseph, just throw it. You don't even like it." I said, "No! I paid for it!" I ate it all, slowly, while we walked, and then my tummy hurt on the ride. I didn't even enjoy the giant wheel. Later I thought: the thirty rupees were gone anyway, whether I ate it or not. Eating it didn't bring them back. It only made the giant wheel worse. Next time I think I'll stop when it stops being nice.

qa.q: How much did the candy floss cost?
qa.a: Thirty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Joseph keep eating after it stopped tasting nice?
qa.a: Joseph felt guilty about wasting something already paid for, so eating it felt right even while it spoiled the day.

qa.q: What does Joseph plan to do next time, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Stop when it stops being nice, because the money is gone either way and eating more only spoils the rest of the fair.

qa.q: How does Sonali see Joseph's choice?

grounding: A child recalls finishing candy floss that had stopped tasting nice because it was paid for, and later seeing the money was gone either way.

passage:
Camp counsellor's note, Day 3, summer camp, Nashik
During free time Kiran started the thousand-piece jigsaw of a ship. After twenty minutes he was yawning and said it was "the most boring puzzle in the world." When Jagdish invited him to the cricket match outside, he refused: "I've already done a whole hour on this. If I stop now it's a waste." He stayed at the table another forty minutes, sighing, placing hardly any pieces, while the others played. At snack time he looked unhappy and said he "didn't get to do anything fun today." I sat with him and asked, "If you walked in now and saw this puzzle, would you start it?" He said no, straight away. Tomorrow I will remind him he can choose again.

qa.q: What did Kiran say when Jagdish invited him to play cricket?
qa.a: "I've already done a whole hour on this. If I stop now it's a waste."

qa.q: Why did Kiran stay at the puzzle even though he was bored?
qa.a: He felt it would be a waste to give up after an hour, so stopping felt worse than staying, even though he was unhappy.

qa.q: Why is the counsellor's question a helpful one?
qa.a: Asking whether he would start the puzzle now makes Kiran judge the choice from this moment, not from the hour already spent.

qa.q: How might Jagdish feel when Kiran refuses to join the match?
qa.a: Jagdish may feel a little disappointed, since he wanted Kiran to play with them.

grounding: A camp counsellor records a boy who keeps doing a puzzle he finds boring because he has already spent an hour on it.

passage: Every evening at six, Darshan took the crowded jeep from the village to the coaching centre in Hosapete, where three years of biology notes waited for him. He hated every hour of it. What he loved was the old radio sets he fixed for half the village on Sundays. When his sister Sharmila asked why he didn't switch to the electronics diploma, he stared out at the paddy. "Appa has paid three years of fees. If I stop now, all that money and all my evenings are wasted." "And if you go on two more years, hating it?" Darshan didn't answer. The jeep driver honked. He picked up his bag of notes and went, as he did every evening, with a heavy chest.

passage: Every Saturday, Kwame walked past the football pitch in Accra where his friends were playing and went into the music school for his violin lesson. Six years of lessons. His aunt had paid for all of them, and his certificates hung on the wall at home. He didn't hate music; he hated the violin, the squeaks, the hours of scales. It would all be for nothing." "Would it?" Soo-ah asked. "You can read music. That doesn't disappear." Kwame stood at the music school door for a long time before going in.

Monday. At Sahil's cousin's engagement, Rajni smiled for photos and felt nothing. They had been together since first year: three years, two anniversaries at the same café, his family already calling her "bahu" as a joke. They hardly talked any more except about exams.
Thursday. Her roommate asked, "Are you happy?" Rajni laughed. "That's not the point. Three years! If I end it now, what were those years for?" She lay awake counting everything she had given: birthdays, Sundays, the trip she skipped for him.
Sunday. On the college steps, Rajni wrote in her notebook: "The three years happened. They were good for a while. They stay good even if I leave." Under it she wrote: "Would I start this today?" She looked at the question for a long time before she called Sahil to ask if they could talk.

qa.q: How long had Rajni and Sahil been together?
qa.a: Since first year: three years.

qa.q: Why did Rajni laugh when asked if she was happy?
qa.a: She felt trapped and uneasy, because admitting unhappiness would make the three years feel wasted, so she brushed the question off.

qa.q: What question does Rajni finally ask herself, and why does it help?

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Rajni asks to talk?

passage: Karthik, you say you can't leave engineering because you've done two years. Listen to your Zeenat aunty for a minute. At nineteen I started a pharmacy degree because my father liked the idea. By second year I knew I hated it; I was happiest editing the college magazine. But I thought, two years, all those fees, all those nights. So I stayed. Third year, fourth year. I passed, just, and worked in a medicine shop for a year feeling like a ghost. At twenty-three I finally started journalism, older than everyone in my class. The two extra years didn't save the first two. They only added two more I didn't want. The day I left, I cried, and then I slept better than I had in years.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat happiest doing in college?
qa.a: Editing the college magazine.

passage: The course-change window closed at five, and it was already 3:40. Irfan sat outside the registrar's office with the form half filled: from B.Com to B.A. Psychology. Dear Pa and Nu,
I've tried to say this on the phone three times and couldn't, so I'm writing it. I don't want to go on with the civil services coaching in Delhi. I know you have spent so much on it: two years of fees, the room, Pa's savings from the shop. I know how proud you were telling everyone at church. That is exactly why I've kept going. passage: Irfan, you asked why Devika still runs a boutique she hates. Okay, honestly. Monday. Gargi's father showed the neighbour the folder: test scores, application fee receipts, the bank letter. "Our Gargi is going to America in August." Gargi smiled and went to her room. She had been offered a job in Pune last week and hadn't told anyone.
Wednesday. Her brother Sahil found her awake at 2 a.m., staring at the visa checklist. "You don't want to go, do you?" "Papa has already spent so much. And he's told everyone. If I say no now, I'm throwing all of it away. Throwing him away." Sahil sat on the floor beside her. "What's spent is spent. What's next is still yours to choose."
Saturday. After dinner, with Sahil beside her, Gargi said, "Papa, can I show you something?" and put the Pune offer letter on the table.

qa.q: Where was Gargi offered a job?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: Why is Gargi awake at 2 a.m. staring at the checklist?
qa.a: She feels trapped and guilty, because her father's spending and pride make saying no feel like throwing him away.

qa.q: What helps Gargi move toward an honest talk?
qa.a: Sahil's support, sitting with her at night and beside her at dinner, so she can show Papa the offer letter kindly and openly.

qa.q: How might Gargi's father feel when he sees the offer letter?
qa.a: He may feel shocked and hurt after telling everyone, but it also gives him a chance to understand what his daughter really wants.

grounding: Over a week, a young woman feels bound to her father's costly plan for her, and with her brother's help begins an honest conversation.

passage: At 9 p.m. the lab at the institute was empty except for Urmila and the hum of the freezer. Two years on the same enzyme project, and the fourth trial had failed exactly like the first three. Her supervisor, Sarika, had left a sticky note: "Decide by Monday: continue, or switch to the soil project?" Urmila sat with her notebook and wrote a single question: If I were starting today, knowing what I know now, would I choose this? She answered honestly: No. She let herself sit with that for a while, eyes stinging. Two years. Then she made a list: what the failures had taught her, which methods she could carry to the soil work. On Monday she told Sarika, "I'm switching. I'll write up what didn't work, so nobody else loses two years." Sarika nodded. "That's a real result too."

qa.q: What did Sarika's sticky note ask?
qa.a: Decide by Monday: continue, or switch to the soil project?

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling when she answered No?
qa.a: She felt sad and grieved the two years, eyes stinging, but she let herself feel it instead of hiding from it.

qa.q: How does Urmila turn the lost time into something useful?
qa.a: She lists what the failures taught her and plans to write up what didn't work, so the cost becomes learning instead of shame.

qa.q: How does Sarika see Urmila's decision?
qa.a: Sarika sees it as sound and even valuable, calling the write-up a real result too.

grounding: A young researcher asks whether she would start her project today, grieves the lost years, keeps the lessons and switches.

passage:
Dear Chaitanya,
I've decided to close the weekend bakery stall. Eighteen months, every Saturday at 4 a.m., and I'm tired in a way sleep doesn't fix. For weeks I thought I couldn't stop, because of the oven I bought and all those Saturdays. Then I asked myself something you once asked me: "If you were starting today, knowing all this, would you?" The honest answer was no. I'd bake for friends, not for a stall.
I cried about it on Sunday. I'm allowed to. It was a real thing I built. But I also learned how to price, how to talk to strangers and how to get up at four without complaining, and I'm keeping all of that.
I'm not ashamed. It did its job. Now I want my Saturdays back.
Come for cake; the oven stays.
Trisha

qa.q: How long did Trisha run the weekend bakery stall?
qa.a: Eighteen months, every Saturday at 4 a.m.

qa.q: How does Trisha feel about closing the stall?
qa.a: Trisha feels sad enough to cry on Sunday, but not ashamed; proud of what was built and relieved at getting Saturdays back.

qa.q: What question helped Trisha decide, and why does it work?
qa.a: "If you were starting today, knowing all this, would you?" It looks forward instead of at the oven and the Saturdays already spent.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Chaitanya may feel touched that an old question helped, and glad to be invited for cake.

grounding: A young worker writes about asking whether they would start the stall today, grieving it and moving on without shame.

passage: Lalit, people expect me to say shutting down the app was the worst day of my life. It wasn't. The worst days were the six months before, when I kept going because of the three years already in it. Every morning I'd open the numbers, see them flat, and think, Avni, you can't quit now, look what you've spent. Then my co-founder asked me one question over chai: "If we had a blank page today, knowing what we know, would we build this?" I said no before I could stop myself. We both went quiet. I grieved it properly: I cried in the car, I sat with the team, I thanked them. Then we wrote down every lesson, and I took them to my next job. No shame in that. Only the six months I wish I'd had back.

qa.q: What did Avni's co-founder ask over chai?
qa.a: If we had a blank page today, knowing what we know, would we build this?

qa.q: What was Avni feeling in the six months before shutting down?
qa.a: Avni felt stuck and weighed down, opening flat numbers every morning but unable to quit because of the three years already spent.

qa.q: How did Avni close the chapter well?
qa.a: By grieving openly, thanking the team, writing down every lesson and carrying them to the next job, without shame.

qa.q: How might the team have felt when Avni sat with them and thanked them?
qa.a: They were probably sad but respected, feeling their work mattered even though the app was closing.

grounding: A young founder describes asking whether they would build the product again today, then grieving it and moving on without shame.

passage: Yesterday I won a blue cat's-eye marble from Tipu in the courtyard. I said "yes!", put it in my tin and went back to playing. That was it. Then, ten minutes later, I lost my red one to Chotu, the red one I've had since Diwali. I cried so much that Vinita didi came down from the terrace. She said, "Naveen, you won one and you lost one. You have the same number of marbles." I know. I counted. But the blue one felt like just a marble, and the red one felt like MINE. Losing it hurt way more than winning felt good. Didi said that's normal and gave me a hug. Today I still looked for the red one in Chotu's pocket.

qa.q: Since when had Naveen had the red marble?
qa.a: Since Diwali.

qa.q: Why did losing the red marble hurt more than winning the blue one felt good?
qa.a: The red one felt like Naveen's own, so losing it brought real hurt and tears, while the new blue one felt like just a marble.

qa.q: How does Vinita didi help, and what else could help Naveen?
qa.a: She points out the count is the same and gives a hug; Naveen could also give the blue marble time to feel special too.

qa.q: How might Chotu feel when Naveen checks his pocket?
qa.a: Chotu may feel a bit uncomfortable or annoyed, since he won the red marble fairly.

grounding: A child recalls crying hard over losing a marble after barely noticing winning an equal one.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 3B, Friday
Something from our reward stars this week is worth recording about Darshan. On Monday he earned a gold star for his reading; he smiled, said "thank you, Miss," and went back to his seat. On Thursday, after talking during the test, he lost one star from his chart. He cried for almost twenty minutes and would not come out at break. Preeti, who sits next to him, told me, "He says it was his best star." It was the same star he had earned on Monday. I sat with him at lunch, told him that feeling upset about losing something is normal, and showed him how he could earn it back by Friday. He did. From now on I will be gentler about taking stars away.

qa.q: What did Darshan earn the gold star for on Monday?
qa.a: For his reading.

qa.q: Why did Darshan cry so much over one lost star?
qa.a: He felt hurt and upset because the star had become his own, so losing it felt far heavier than earning it had felt good.

qa.q: What did the teacher do that helped Darshan?
qa.a: Sat with him at lunch, said feeling upset about losing is normal, and showed him a way to earn the star back by Friday.

qa.q: How does Preeti seem to see Darshan's upset?
qa.a: Preeti seems concerned for him, explaining to the teacher that he calls it his best star.

grounding: A teacher records a boy who barely reacts to earning a star but cries hard when he loses the same star.

passage:
Tuesday
Today I found a ten-rupee coin under the bench in the park. I was happy for about one minute and then I forgot about it.
In the evening Pradeep and I went to buy samosas, and I found out I had lost my own ten-rupee note, the one Nani gave me on Sunday. I was SO upset. I looked everywhere, even inside my socks. I didn't want my samosa. Pradeep said, "But you found ten rupees this morning, so it's the same." I know it's the same. Maths says it's the same. But the coin was just lucky, and the note was mine, from Nani. Losing it felt like losing something from my pocket and my heart.
Tomorrow I'll check under the bench again, just in case.
Deepak

qa.q: Who gave Deepak the ten-rupee note?
qa.a: Nani, on Sunday.

qa.q: Why was Deepak so upset about the note when a coin had been found the same day?
qa.a: The note felt like Deepak's own, from Nani, so losing it hurt far more than finding the lucky coin felt good.

qa.q: What could help Deepak feel better about the lost note?
qa.a: Telling Nani how much the note meant, and letting the coin found that morning feel like a small gift too.

qa.q: How does Pradeep see the loss?
qa.a: Pradeep sees it as even, since ten rupees were found and ten were lost, and is puzzled that Deepak is so upset.

grounding: A child's diary shows losing a ten-rupee note hurting far more than finding an equal coin felt good.

passage: This year, when the basketball coach asked me to try out, I said no without thinking. I'm the captain of our school chess team. Everyone knows me as the chess one; I've won three inter-school trophies. In basketball I'd be the worst player on the court, and the thought of people laughing made my stomach turn. My friend Alka joined the team in June having never touched a ball. She was terrible at first. Now she's in the starting five, and she has a whole new group of friends. Sometimes I watch their practice from the library window. I didn't lose anything by saying no. But I didn't gain anything either. Maybe next term, Ujjwal will ask the coach again.

qa.q: How many inter-school chess trophies has Ujjwal won?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: Why did Ujjwal say no to basketball without thinking?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt afraid of losing standing as chess captain and of people laughing, which felt worse than anything basketball might offer.

qa.q: What small step could Ujjwal take next term?
qa.a: Ask the coach for one practice session just to try, since being bad at first is exactly how Alka started.

qa.q: How has trying basketball changed things for Alka?
qa.a: Alka went from terrible to the starting five and made a whole new group of friends.

grounding: A teenager recalls refusing a new sport because losing status as chess captain felt worse than any possible gain.

passage:
School counsellor's note, Thursday
Francis (Class 10) came in to talk about the drama club. He told me he has wanted to act since Class 7 and that Elizabeth, who runs the club, has asked him twice. Each time he said no. His reason: his current group of friends "think drama is for losers," and he is worried that if he joins, he will lose his place with them and "end up with nobody." He said this even though he admitted he is often bored with the group and laughs at jokes he doesn't like. We talked about what he might gain, not only what he might lose. He agreed to watch one rehearsal on Monday without committing. I will check in with him after that.

qa.q: How many times has Elizabeth asked Francis to join?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: What is Francis worried about if he joins the drama club?
qa.a: He is worried and afraid of losing his place with his current friends and ending up with nobody, which feels bigger than the chance to act.

qa.q: Why is watching one rehearsal a good step?
qa.a: It lets Francis try the new group without giving anything up yet, so he can see the possible gain for himself.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth feel after asking twice?
qa.a: Elizabeth may feel a little disappointed but still hopeful, since she keeps inviting him.

grounding: A counsellor records a teenage boy who avoids the drama club because losing his place in his current group feels worse than the gain.

passage:
Friday
Papa showed me the letter again tonight. The big school in the city has offered me a seat in the science batch, with the olympiad coaching I always wanted. I said I'll think. I've been "thinking" for three weeks.
Here I'm first in class. Every teacher knows my name. Ujjwal and I sit on the last bench, and everyone asks us for notes. In the city school I might be thirtieth. What if I'm just average there? What if nobody even knows who I am?
Ujjwal says, "You'll be learning from people better than you, that's the whole point." I know he's right. But being first feels so safe.
The reply is due Monday.
Anand

qa.q: What does the city school offer Anand?
qa.a: A seat in the science batch, with the olympiad coaching.

qa.q: Why has Anand been thinking it over for three weeks?
qa.a: Anand feels afraid of losing the safe spot as first in class and of being average and unknown, which feels heavier than the chance to learn more.

qa.q: What could help Anand decide by Monday?
qa.a: Listing what could be gained, such as learning from people better at science, next to what could be lost, and talking it through with Papa and a teacher.

qa.q: How does Ujjwal see the offer?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees it as a real chance to learn from better people, which he thinks is the whole point.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows delaying a better school offer because losing the top rank feels worse than any gain.
